claims.source: Application of CNO (1 µM) to activate the inhibitory DREADD was found to decrease the tonic firing of Pitx2+ interneurons in slices from Pitx2::Cre;tdTomato;hM4Di mice (Figure 2b, t(8)=6.08, Paired t-test, p=0.0003).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: CNO did not change spontaneous firing frequencies in slices from Pitx2::Cre;tdTomato mice that do not express the hM4Di receptor.
claims.source: In slices from Pitx2::Cre;tdTomato mice, which express the red fluorescent reporter in Pitx2+ interneurons but not the hM4Di receptor, CNO did not change spontaneous firing frequencies (Figure 2c, t(4)=0.53, Paired t-test, p=0.6228), confirming that the actions of CNO were selective to the hM4Di receptor.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through control experiments shown in Figure 2c.

claims.claim: Inhibition of Pitx2+ interneurons during fictive locomotion did not change burst frequency.
claims.source: Inhibition of Pitx2+ interneurons during fictive locomotion did not change burst frequency (Q = 0.57, Friedman's test, p=0.7515; Figure 3c, n = 14) or duration (Q = 5.28, Friedman's test, p=0.0712; Figure 3e, n = 14) but significantly decreased burst amplitude (−10.7 ± 1.8%, F = 4.34, Repeated measures ANOVA, p=0.0235; Figure 3g, n = 14).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through ventral root recordings shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Inhibition of Pitx2+ interneurons during fictive locomotion did not change burst duration.
claims.source: Inhibition of Pitx2+ interneurons during fictive locomotion did not change burst frequency (Q = 0.57, Friedman's test, p=0.7515; Figure 3c, n = 14) or duration (Q = 5.28, Friedman's test, p=0.0712; Figure 3e, n = 14) but significantly decreased burst amplitude (−10.7 ± 1.8%, F = 4.34, Repeated measures ANOVA, p=0.0235; Figure 3g, n = 14).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through ventral root recordings shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Inhibition of Pitx2+ interneurons during fictive locomotion significantly decreased burst amplitude by 10.7%.
claims.source: Inhibition of Pitx2+ interneurons during fictive locomotion did not change burst frequency (Q = 0.57, Friedman's test, p=0.7515; Figure 3c, n = 14) or duration (Q = 5.28, Friedman's test, p=0.0712; Figure 3e, n = 14) but significantly decreased burst amplitude (−10.7 ± 1.8%, F = 4.34, Repeated measures ANOVA, p=0.0235; Figure 3g, n = 14).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through ventral root recordings shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: When M2 receptors were blocked using methoctramine, DREADD-mediated inhibition of Pitx2+ interneurons had no significant effect on burst frequency, duration or amplitude.
claims.source: When M2 receptors were blocked using methoctramine (10 µM; Figure 3b), DREADD-mediated inhibition of Pitx2+ interneurons had no significant effect on burst frequency (F = 1.23, Repeated measures ANOVA, p=0.3203; Figure 3d, n = 8), duration (Q = 3.25, Friedman's test, p=0.2359; Figure 3f, n = 8) or amplitude (F = 0.89, Repeated measures ANOVA, p=0.4345, Figure 3h, n = 8), indicating that the observed reduction in motor output involved C-boutons derived from V0c interneurons.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through ventral root recordings with M2 receptor blockade shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Application of CNO to chemogenetically inhibit Pitx2+ interneurons led to a reduction in the rate of motoneuron firing during locomotor bursts.
claims.source: Application of CNO, to chemogenetically inhibit Pitx2+ interneurons, led to a clear reduction in the rate of motoneuron firing during locomotor bursts (t(3)=5.40, Paired t-test, p=0.0125; Figure 4b).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: An outward current of 102 ± 14 pA was observed in motoneurons when CNO was applied to inhibit Pitx2+ interneurons.
claims.source: We also observed an outward current in motoneurons when CNO was applied (102 ± 14 pA, n = 11), which was associated with a decrease in input resistance (control: 88 ± 8 MΩ, CNO: 68 ± 4 MΩ, t(8)=2.455, Paired t-test, p=0.0386).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through voltage-clamp recordings.

claims.claim: Efficient ablation of Pitx2+/ChAT+ V0c interneurons was achieved in Pitx2::Cre;vAChT-stop-DTA mice.
claims.source: Immunohistochemical analysis in both neonatal (P2; Figure 5a and P7; Figure 5b–d) and young adult (P25; Figure 5e) transgenic mice demonstrated efficient ablation of Pitx2+/ChAT+ V0c interneurons in Pitx2::Cre;vAChT-stop-DTA and Pitx2::Cre;tdTomato;vAChT-stop-DTA mice (t(4)=8.42, Unpaired t-test, p=0.0011; Figure 5d).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: 95.8% of C-bouton synapses were deleted in Pitx2::Cre;tdTomato;vAChT-stop-DTA mice.
claims.source: C-bouton counts from pictures of 50 randomly selected motoneurons from the control group (n = 3 Pitx2::Cre;tdTomato) and pictures of 50 randomly selected motoneurons from the experimental group (n = 3 Pitx2::Cre;tdTomato;vAChT-stop-DTA) revealed 381 synapses in the control tissue and 16 synapses in the experimental tissue (95.8% deletion).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through quantitative analysis of immunohistochemistry.

claims.claim: In wild-type mice, blockade of M2 receptors via application of methoctramine reduced the amplitude of locomotor-related ventral root bursting by 16.8%.
claims.source: In wild-type mice (Figure 6a), blockade of M2 receptors via application of methoctramine reduced the amplitude of locomotor-related ventral root bursting (−16.8 ± 4.1%, Q = 9.50, Friedman's test, p=0.0087; Figure 6g, n = 12), decreased burst frequency (−11.9 ± 3.6%, Q = 11.62, Friedman's test, p=0.0030; Figure 6c, n = 12) and increased burst duration (27.2 ± 3.4%, Q = 20.67, Friedman's test, p<0.0001; Figure 6e, n = 12), similar to recently reported effects of M2 receptor antagonists on whole cord output in neonatal mice (Nascimento et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through ventral root recordings shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: In wild-type mice, blockade of M2 receptors decreased burst frequency by 11.9%.
claims.source: In wild-type mice (Figure 6a), blockade of M2 receptors via application of methoctramine reduced the amplitude of locomotor-related ventral root bursting (−16.8 ± 4.1%, Q = 9.50, Friedman's test, p=0.0087; Figure 6g, n = 12), decreased burst frequency (−11.9 ± 3.6%, Q = 11.62, Friedman's test, p=0.0030; Figure 6c, n = 12) and increased burst duration (27.2 ± 3.4%, Q = 20.67, Friedman's test, p<0.0001; Figure 6e, n = 12), similar to recently reported effects of M2 receptor antagonists on whole cord output in neonatal mice (Nascimento et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through ventral root recordings shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: In wild-type mice, blockade of M2 receptors increased burst duration by 27.2%.
claims.source: In wild-type mice (Figure 6a), blockade of M2 receptors via application of methoctramine reduced the amplitude of locomotor-related ventral root bursting (−16.8 ± 4.1%, Q = 9.50, Friedman's test, p=0.0087; Figure 6g, n = 12), decreased burst frequency (−11.9 ± 3.6%, Q = 11.62, Friedman's test, p=0.0030; Figure 6c, n = 12) and increased burst duration (27.2 ± 3.4%, Q = 20.67, Friedman's test, p<0.0001; Figure 6e, n = 12), similar to recently reported effects of M2 receptor antagonists on whole cord output in neonatal mice (Nascimento et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through ventral root recordings shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Methoctramine no longer had an effect on burst amplitude when V0c interneurons and C-boutons were ablated in Pitx2::Cre;vAChT-stop-DTA mice.
claims.source: However, methoctramine no longer had an effect on burst amplitude when V0c interneurons and C-boutons were ablated (2.3 ± 2.2%, F = 0.32, Friedman's test, p=0.7263; Figure 6h, n = 10).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through ventral root recordings in ablation mice shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: V0c interneurons and their C-bouton contacts with motoneurons are solely responsible for the M2 muscarinic receptor-mediated modulation of the intensity of locomotor-related output.
claims.source: These data demonstrate that V0c interneurons and their C-bouton contacts with motoneurons are solely responsible for the M2 muscarinic receptor-mediated modulation of the intensity of locomotor-related output.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the ablation experiments shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Application of CNO reliably increased the spontaneous firing frequency of Pitx2+ interneurons in spinal cord slices prepared from Pitx2::Cre;tdTomato;hM3Dq mice.
claims.source: Application of CNO reliably increased the spontaneous firing frequency of Pitx2+ interneurons clustered near the central canal in spinal cord slices prepared from Pitx2::Cre;tdTomato;hM3Dq mice (t(7)=2.45, Paired t-test, p=0.0441; Figure 7a).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 7a.

claims.claim: Activation of Pitx2+ interneurons with CNO elicited an inward current of -37 ± 6 pA in motoneurons from Pitx2::Cre;hM3Dq mice.
claims.source: In spinal cords from Pitx2::Cre;hM3Dq mice, activation of Pitx2+ interneurons with CNO elicited an inward current in motoneurons (−37 ± 6 pA, n = 14; Figure 7b left) that was associated with an increase in input resistance (control: 77 ± 9 MΩ, CNO: 90 ± 12 MΩ, W=-46, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.0217,n = 10).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 7b.

claims.claim: The M2 receptor antagonist methoctramine blocked the inward current induced by CNO activation of Pitx2+ interneurons.
claims.source: The M2 receptor antagonist methoctramine, blocked both this inward current (−2 ± 4 pA, n = 9; Figure 6b, middle) and the change in input resistance (methoctramine: 82 ± 13 MΩ, methoctramine+CNO: 89 ± 16 MΩ, t(7)=1.68, Paired t-test, p=0.1368, n = 8), supporting that these CNO-induced effects involve V0c interneurons and their C-boutons.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through voltage-clamp recordings with M2 receptor blockade shown in Figure 7b.

claims.claim: Co-application of CNO with guangxitoxin-1E still induced an inward current of -30 ± 7 pA, indicating that Kv2.1 channels are not involved in this response.
claims.source: Co-application of CNO with guangxitoxin-1E still induced an inward current (−30 ± 7 pA, n = 10; Figure 7b, right) that was associated with an increase in input resistance (guangxitoxin-1E: 49 ± 5 MΩ, guangxitoxin-1E and CNO: 58 ± 3 MΩ, t(7)=3.28, Paired t-test, p=0.0135, n = 8), indicating that Kv2.1 channels are not involved in this response.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through voltage-clamp recordings with Kv2.1 channel blockade shown in Figure 7b.

claims.claim: Activation of Pitx2+ interneurons with CNO decreased motoneuron rheobase.
claims.source: Activation of Pitx2+ interneurons with CNO (Figure 7c) decreased motoneuron rheobase (t(22)=3.32, Paired t-test, p=0.0031), increased the current required to reach a depolarizing block of firing (W=-148, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.0054) and increased the maximum firing rate of motoneurons (t(23)=4.13, Paired t-test, p=0.0004).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 7c.

claims.claim: Activation of Pitx2+ interneurons with CNO increased the current required to reach a depolarizing block of firing.
claims.source: Activation of Pitx2+ interneurons with CNO (Figure 7c) decreased motoneuron rheobase (t(22)=3.32, Paired t-test, p=0.0031), increased the current required to reach a depolarizing block of firing (W=-148, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.0054) and increased the maximum firing rate of motoneurons (t(23)=4.13, Paired t-test, p=0.0004).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 7c.

claims.claim: Activation of Pitx2+ interneurons with CNO increased the maximum firing rate of motoneurons.
claims.source: Activation of Pitx2+ interneurons with CNO (Figure 7c) decreased motoneuron rheobase (t(22)=3.32, Paired t-test, p=0.0031), increased the current required to reach a depolarizing block of firing (W=-148, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.0054) and increased the maximum firing rate of motoneurons (t(23)=4.13, Paired t-test, p=0.0004).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 7c.

claims.claim: When M2 receptors were blocked with methoctramine, activation of Pitx2+ interneurons had no effect on motoneuron rheobase, depolarizing block or maximum firing rates.
claims.source: When M2 receptors were blocked with methoctramine (Figure 7d) activation of Pitx2+ interneurons had no effect on motoneuron rheobase (t(10)=0.04, Paired t-test, p=0.9709), depolarizing block (t(10)=0.000, Paired t-test, p=1.0000) or maximum firing rates (W = 19.00, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.3552).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through current-clamp recordings with M2 receptor blockade shown in Figure 7d.

claims.claim: Activation of Pitx2+ interneurons in the presence of the Kv2.1 blocker guangxitoxin-E still reduced motoneuron rheobase but no longer affected the current required for a depolarizing block nor motoneuron maximum firing rates.
claims.source: Activation of Pitx2+ interneurons in the presence of the Kv2.1 blocker guangxitoxin-E, still reduced motoneuron rheobase (t(13)=2.47, Paired t-test, p=0.0279), but no longer affected the current required for a depolarizing block (W = −21.00, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.3532) nor motoneuron maximum firing rates (t(13)=0.000, Paired t-test, p=1.0000).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through current-clamp recordings with Kv2.1 channel blockade shown in Figure 7e.

claims.claim: Chemogenetic activation of Pitx2+ interneurons increases the firing output of motoneurons through activation of M2 receptors and subsequent regulation of Kv2.1 channels.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that chemogenetic activation of Pitx2+ interneurons increases the firing output of motoneurons through activation of M2 receptors and subsequent regulation of Kv2.1 channels that are present at C-bouton synapses.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the experiments shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Activation of Pitx2+ interneurons with CNO decreased motoneuron firing threshold measured from ramps.
claims.source: Activation of Pitx2+ interneurons with CNO decreased motoneuron firing threshold measured from ramps (W = 62.00, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.0029; Figure 8a), an effect which was blocked by methoctramine (t(3)=0.67, Paired t-test, p=0.5513; Figure 8b), but not by guangxitoxin1-E (t(5)=3.10, Paired t-test, p=0.0362; Figure 8c).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through current ramp experiments shown in Figure 8a-c.

claims.claim: Activation of M2 receptors at C-bouton synapses reduces the current required for motoneuron firing by hyperpolarizing the action potential threshold via Kv2.1-independent mechanisms.
claims.source: These data indicate that activation of M2 receptors at C-bouton synapses reduces the current required for motoneuron firing by hyperpolarizing the action potential threshold via Kv2.1-independent mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the threshold experiments shown in Figure 8a-c.

claims.claim: Activation of Pitx2+ interneurons with CNO increased the mAHP amplitude.
claims.source: Surprisingly, activation of Pitx2+ interneurons with CNO increased the mAHP amplitude (W = 204, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.0010; Figure 8d).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through single action potential recordings shown in Figure 8d.

claims.claim: The CNO-induced increase in mAHP amplitude was blocked when CNO was co-applied with either methoctramine or guangxitoxin1-E.
claims.source: This effect was blocked when CNO was co-applied with either the M2 receptor antagonist methoctramine (t(6)=0.63, Paired t-test, p=0.5513; Figure 8e) or the Kv2.1 channel blocker guangxitoxin1-E (t(15)=1.27, Paired t-test, p=0.2208; Figure 8f).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through single action potential recordings with receptor/channel blockade shown in Figure 8e-f.

claims.claim: An increase in the amplitude of inter-spike AHPs in motoneurons was observed following activation of Pitx2+ interneurons with CNO.
claims.source: We observed an increase in the amplitude of inter-spike AHPs in motoneurons following activation of Pitx2+ interneurons with CNO (t(20)=8.44, Paired t-test, p<0.0001; Figure 8g).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through repetitive firing recordings shown in Figure 8g.

claims.claim: The increase in inter-spike AHP amplitude was blocked by both methoctramine and guangxitoxin1-E.
claims.source: This effect was blocked by both the M2 receptor antagonist methoctramine (t(9)=1.02, Paired t-test, p=0.3354; Figure 8h) and the Kv2.1 blocker guangxitoxin1-E (t(11)=1.45, Paired t-test, p=0.1736; Figure 8i).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through repetitive firing recordings with receptor/channel blockade shown in Figure 8h-i.

claims.claim: C-bouton activation enables motoneurons to fire during sustained and intense stimulation by increasing the inter-spike AHP.
claims.source: These data indicate that C-bouton activation enables motoneurons to fire during sustained and intense stimulation by increasing the inter-spike AHP.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the inter-spike AHP experiments shown in Figure 8g-i.

claims.claim: Activation of Pitx2+ interneurons with CNO decreased spike half-width.
claims.source: Activation of Pitx2+ interneurons with CNO decreased spike half-width (W = 182, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.0007; Figure 8j).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through single action potential recordings shown in Figure 8j.

claims.claim: The decrease in spike half-width was blocked by both methoctramine and guangxitoxin1-E.
claims.source: This effect was blocked by both the M2 receptor antagonist methoctramine (W=-42, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.0674; Figure 8k) and the Kv2.1 blocker guangxitoxin1-E (t(12)=1.10, Paired t-test, p=0.2951; Figure 8l).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through single action potential recordings with receptor/channel blockade shown in Figure 8k-l.

claims.claim: M2 receptor-mediated modulation of Kv2.1 channels at C-bouton synapses facilitates greater motoneuron firing rates by reducing spike half-width.
claims.source: These observations demonstrate that M2 receptor-mediated modulation of Kv2.1 channels at C-bouton synapses also facilitates greater motoneuron firing rates by reducing spike half-width.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the spike half-width experiments shown in Figure 8j-l.

claims.claim: Recruitment of V0c interneurons and their C-bouton synapses leads to activation of postsynaptic M2 receptors, which in turn regulate Kv2.1 channel function to facilitate increased and sustained motoneuron firing.
claims.source: By combining Ca2+ imaging, chemogenetic manipulation and conditional ablation of cholinergic Pitx2+ interneurons (V0c), we demonstrate that recruitment of V0c interneurons and their C-bouton synapses leads to activation of postsynaptic M2 receptors, which in turn regulate Kv2.1 channel function to facilitate increased and sustained motoneuron firing.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all experimental data.

claims.claim: Activation of the V0c system results in augmented motor output that will translate into stronger muscle activity.
claims.source: Thus, activation of the V0c system results in augmented motor output that will translate into stronger muscle activity.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the overall findings of the study.

claims.claim: V0c interneurons receive synaptic inputs from sensory pathways, supraspinal structures and CPG networks.
claims.source: V0c interneurons receive synaptic inputs from a range of sources, including sensory pathways, supraspinal structures and CPG networks (Figure 9; Zagoraiou et al., 2009; Stepien et al., 2010; Murray et al., 2018), which 'mirror' inputs received by motoneurons and are therefore relevant to desired motor output.
claims.evidence: This is stated with supporting citations and illustrated in Figure 9.

claims.claim: The C-bouton system is less active during regular motor tasks such as walking but is particularly important during locomotor behaviors that require increased muscle activation such as swimming.
claims.source: The C-bouton system seems to be less active during regular motor tasks such as walking but is particularly important during locomotor behaviors that require increased muscle activation such as swimming (Zagoraiou et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: V0c interneurons represent one functionally distinct neuromodulatory module devoted to task-dependent control of the intensity of motor output.
claims.source: We provide evidence in support of a modular architecture for spinal cholinergic systems, in line with that recently proposed for the locus coerleus (Chandler et al., 2019; Totah et al., 2018), where V0c interneurons represent one functionally distinct neuromodulatory module devoted to task-dependent control of the intensity of motor output.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the study's findings with reference to similar organizational principles in other systems.

claims.claim: The majority of Pitx2+ interneurons are tonically active at rest.
claims.source: As previously reported, the majority of Pitx2+ interneurons were tonically active at rest (Zagoraiou et al., 2009; Figure 2b,c).
claims.evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Pitx2+ interneurons are distinctively clustered around the central canal.
claims.source: Pitx2+ cells express both the hM4Di inhibitory receptor and the tdTomato red fluorescent reporter, which allowed them to be identified for single-cell electrophysiology (Figure 2a). Pitx2+ interneurons, which are distinctively clustered around the central canal, were targeted for recordings (Zagoraiou et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: M2 receptors are not only juxtaposed to C-boutons but are also widely distributed throughout motoneuron somata.
claims.source: Given that M2 receptors are not only juxtaposed to C-boutons but are also widely distributed throughout motoneuron somata (Wilson et al., 2004; Miles et al., 2007; Hellström et al., 2003; Welton et al., 1999) and on spinal interneurons (Höglund and Baghdoyan, 1997), it is likely that additional, as yet genetically undefined, neuronal sources of intraspinal acetylcholine (Bertrand and Cazalets, 2011; Gillberg et al., 1988; Gillberg et al., 1990; Sherriff and Henderson, 1994) are responsible for these M2 receptor-dependent changes in the rhythm and pattern of locomotor output.
claims.evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claims.claim: There are additional, as yet genetically undefined, neuronal sources of intraspinal acetylcholine.
claims.source: Given that M2 receptors are not only juxtaposed to C-boutons but are also widely distributed throughout motoneuron somata (Wilson et al., 2004; Miles et al., 2007; Hellström et al., 2003; Welton et al., 1999) and on spinal interneurons (Höglund and Baghdoyan, 1997), it is likely that additional, as yet genetically undefined, neuronal sources of intraspinal acetylcholine (Bertrand and Cazalets, 2011; Gillberg et al., 1988; Gillberg et al., 1990; Sherriff and Henderson, 1994) are responsible for these M2 receptor-dependent changes in the rhythm and pattern of locomotor output.
claims.evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claims.claim: SK channel clusters preferentially appose large cholinergic C-bouton terminals.
claims.source: SK channel clusters preferentially appose large cholinergic C-bouton terminals (Deardorff, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: SK channels are distributed throughout laminae VII and IX.
claims.source: However, SK channels are also distributed throughout laminae VII and IX, and could therefore be present on more distal motoneuron dendrites where they might be subject to modulation by as yet uncharacterized, Pitx2-negative, populations of cholinergic spinal interneurons (Bertrand and Cazalets, 2011; Gillberg et al., 1988; Gillberg et al., 1990; Sherriff and Henderson, 1994; Deardorff, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Dephosphorylation of Kv2.1 channels in response to prolonged excitatory drive causes channel delustering in motoneurons.
claims.source: Kv2.1 dephosphorylation in response to prolonged excitatory drive is thought to cause channel delustering in motoneurons, whilst reduced activity can increase Kv2.1 channel clustering (Romer et al., 2019; Romer et al., 2016; Romer et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claims.claim: In motoneurons, declustering of Kv2.1 channels occurs in response to increased glutamatergic, but not cholinergic, input.
claims.source: Interestingly, in motoneurons, declustering occurs in response to increased glutamatergic, but not cholinergic, input (Romer et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: Activation of C-boutons has been proposed to maintain Kv2.1 clusters and promote repetitive firing at physiological activity levels.
claims.source: Thus, activation of C-boutons should not lead to declustering of Kv2.1 channels and has in fact been proposed to maintain Kv2.1 clusters and promote repetitive firing at physiological activity levels (Romer et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: Dephosphorylation of Kv2.1 channels leads to a hyperpolarizing shift in channel activation and inactivation properties in hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: Although data are lacking for motoneurons, dephosphorylation of Kv2.1 channels leads to a hyperpolarizing shift in channel activation and inactivation properties in hippocampal neurons, which is thought to suppress action potential firing frequency (Mohapatra and Trimmer, 2006; Mohapatra et al., 2009; Misonou et al., 2005; Park et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claims.claim: The overall pre- and post-synaptic components of C-bouton synapses, including M2 receptors and Kv2.1 channels, appear to remain consistent from early neonatal stages into adulthood.
claims.source: The overall pre- and post-synaptic components of C-bouton synapses, including M2 receptors and Kv2.1 channels, appear to remain consistent from early neonatal stages into adulthood (Zagoraiou et al., 2009; Wilson et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Postnatal maturation of C-boutons involves increased clustering of Kv2.1 channels and M2 receptors along with an increase in the size of C-boutons until motor networks become functionally mature (~P15).
claims.source: Rather than changes in the major components, postnatal maturation of C-boutons involves increased clustering of Kv2.1 channels and M2 receptors along with an increase in the size of C-boutons until motor networks become functionally mature (~P15) (Wilson et al., 2004; Phelps et al., 1984; Wetts and Vaughn, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Genetic perturbation of C-boutons in adult mice impairs the ability of motoneurons to increase muscle activation in response to behavioral demands.
claims.source: However, the fact that genetic perturbation of C-boutons in adult mice impairs the ability of motoneurons to increase muscle activation in response to behavioral demands (Zagoraiou et al., 2009), supports a consistency in the cellular effects of the C-bouton system into adulthood.
claims.evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: Recordings from adult motoneurons within in vivo preparations have shown state-dependent changes in motoneuron properties including a decrease in AHP amplitude, hyperpolarization of action potential threshold, and a small increase in action potential half-width.
claims.source: Recordings from adult motoneurons within in vivo preparations, and associated modelling studies, have shown state-dependent changes in motoneuron properties including a decrease in AHP amplitude, hyperpolarization of action potential threshold, and a small increase in action potential half-width (Power et al., 2010; MacDonell et al., 2015; Krawitz et al., 2001; Brownstone et al., 1992; Dai et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claims.claim: At 50 nM concentration, guangxitoxin-1E is thought to be highly selective for Kv2.1 channels, with limited impact on other channels including Kv4 channels.
claims.source: At this concentration, guangxitoxin-1E is thought to be highly selective for Kv2.1 channels, with limited impact on other channels including Kv4 channels (Herrington et al., 2006; Liu and Bean, 2014; Fletcher et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Kv2 channels permit greater motoneuron firing frequencies by maintaining hyperpolarized inter-spike membrane potentials.
claims.source: This Kv2.1 channel-dependent mechanism is also supported by recent work in rat lumbar motoneurons, which has demonstrated that Kv2 channels permit greater motoneuron firing frequencies by maintaining hyperpolarized inter-spike membrane potentials (Romer et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: Blockade of Kv2 channels increases action potential half-width and slows motoneuron firing.
claims.source: This is again consistent with recent reports of increased action potential half-width and a slowing of motoneuron firing when Kv2 channels are blocked (Romer et al., 2019; Fletcher et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

results.result: Pitx2+ interneurons are rhythmically active during fictive locomotion, with 65.6% of L1-3 interneurons and 31.6% of L4-6 interneurons phase-locked to ventral root output.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C30, and C31 are supported by Ca2+ imaging data (Figure 1) with appropriate statistical analysis (Rayleigh test). The methodology is sound, sample sizes are reported (32 upper lumbar, 19 lower lumbar interneurons from 6 hemisected cords, 3 mice), and the phase-locking analysis is appropriate for assessing rhythmic coupling.

results.result: CNO application via inhibitory DREADD (hM4Di) effectively and selectively decreased tonic firing of Pitx2+ interneurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C32 and C33 demonstrate proper validation of the DREADD approach with appropriate controls. The effect is statistically significant (p=0.0003) in DREADD-expressing mice and absent in controls (p=0.6228), confirming specificity. Sample sizes are adequate (n=9 and n=5).

results.result: Chemogenetic inhibition of Pitx2+ interneurons during fictive locomotion selectively reduces burst amplitude by 10.7% without affecting frequency or duration, and this effect is M2 receptor-dependent.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 are well-supported by ventral root recordings (Figure 3) and motoneuron recordings (Figure 4) with appropriate statistical tests and adequate sample sizes (n=14 for ventral root, n=8 with methoctramine). The M2 receptor dependency is demonstrated by loss of effect with methoctramine blockade. The specificity is confirmed by control experiments showing no CNO effect in non-DREADD mice.

results.result: Genetic ablation of V0c interneurons in Pitx2::Cre;vAChT-stop-DTA mice was highly efficient, achieving 95.8% deletion of C-bouton synapses.
results.evaluation: Claims C40 and C41 are supported by immunohistochemical analysis across multiple developmental stages (P2, P7, P25) with quantitative assessment. The statistical significance (p=0.0011) and high deletion efficiency (95.8%) are well-documented. The methodology includes appropriate controls and adequate sample sizes (n=3 per group, 50 motoneurons analyzed per group).

results.result: V0c interneurons and C-boutons are solely responsible for M2 receptor-mediated modulation of locomotor output amplitude, as demonstrated by loss of methoctramine effect on burst amplitude in ablation mice while effects on frequency and duration persist.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C46 are supported by systematic comparison of methoctramine effects in wild-type versus ablation mice (Figure 6). The selective loss of amplitude modulation (p=0.7263 in ablation vs p=0.0087 in WT) while frequency and duration effects persist demonstrates specificity. Sample sizes are adequate (n=12 WT, n=10 ablation) with appropriate statistical tests.

results.result: Chemogenetic activation of Pitx2+ interneurons induces an M2 receptor-dependent inward current in motoneurons that is independent of Kv2.1 channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 are supported by patch-clamp recordings (Figure 7a-b) with appropriate pharmacological controls. The M2 receptor dependency is confirmed by methoctramine blockade, and Kv2.1 independence is shown by persistence with guangxitoxin-1E. Sample sizes are adequate (n=8-14) with appropriate statistical tests showing significant effects.

results.result: Activation of Pitx2+ interneurons increases motoneuron excitability through M2 receptor-mediated regulation of Kv2.1 channels, decreasing rheobase, increasing depolarizing block threshold, and increasing maximum firing rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C56 are supported by systematic current-clamp experiments (Figure 7c-e) with appropriate pharmacological dissection. The M2 receptor dependency is confirmed by methoctramine blockade, and Kv2.1 involvement in depolarizing block and maximum firing (but not rheobase) is demonstrated by guangxitoxin-1E experiments. Sample sizes are adequate (n=11-23) with appropriate statistical tests.

results.result: Activation of M2 receptors at C-boutons hyperpolarizes action potential threshold through Kv2.1-independent mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58 are supported by current ramp experiments (Figure 8a-c) showing threshold hyperpolarization that is blocked by methoctramine but not guangxitoxin-1E. This demonstrates M2 receptor dependency and Kv2.1 independence. Sample sizes are adequate (n=4-12) with appropriate statistical tests.

results.result: Activation of Pitx2+ interneurons increases mAHP amplitude through M2 receptor and Kv2.1 channel-dependent mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C60 are supported by single action potential recordings (Figure 8d-f) showing increased mAHP that is blocked by both methoctramine and guangxitoxin-1E. This finding is noted as surprising and contrasts with previous literature expectations. Sample sizes are adequate (n=7-22) with appropriate statistical tests.

results.result: C-bouton activation increases inter-spike AHP amplitude through M2 receptor and Kv2.1 channel-dependent mechanisms, enabling sustained motoneuron firing during intense stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 are supported by repetitive firing recordings (Figure 8g-i) showing increased inter-spike AHP that is blocked by both methoctramine and guangxitoxin-1E. The interpretation that this enables sustained firing is reasonable given the biophysical role of inter-spike AHP. Sample sizes are adequate (n=10-21) with appropriate statistical tests.

results.result: M2 receptor-mediated modulation of Kv2.1 channels reduces spike half-width, facilitating greater motoneuron firing rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by single action potential recordings (Figure 8j-l) showing decreased spike half-width that is blocked by both methoctramine and guangxitoxin-1E. The mechanistic link to increased firing rates is consistent with biophysical principles. Sample sizes are adequate (n=11-20) with appropriate statistical tests.

results.result: V0c interneurons modulate motor output through a pathway involving M2 receptor activation and Kv2.1 channel regulation, resulting in increased and sustained motoneuron firing that translates to stronger muscle activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 represent the main conclusion integrating all experimental findings. The pathway from V0c activation through M2 receptors to Kv2.1 modulation is well-supported by the combined Ca2+ imaging, chemogenetic, ablation, and electrophysiological data. The inference to muscle activity is reasonable though not directly tested in this study.

results.result: Background knowledge about spinal motor circuits, V0 interneurons, Pitx2+ interneurons, and C-boutons is established from prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C10-C29 represent established knowledge from prior literature, appropriately cited. These provide necessary context for the current study and are not novel findings. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are consistent with the field.

results.result: V0c interneurons represent a functionally distinct neuromodulatory module that receives diverse inputs and provides task-dependent control of motor output intensity.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 integrate current findings with prior literature to propose a modular architecture for spinal cholinergic systems. The input diversity (C69) and task-dependent activation (C70) are supported by citations. The modular architecture concept (C71) is a reasonable synthesis supported by the current data showing specificity of V0c function.

results.result: Discussion of prior work on Pitx2+ interneuron properties, M2 receptor distribution, SK and Kv2.1 channel function, C-bouton development, and limitations of neonatal preparations.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C88 represent discussion points integrating current findings with prior literature. These are appropriately cited and provide important context for interpreting the results, including discussion of potential mechanisms (C78-C81), developmental considerations (C82-C84), and methodological limitations (C85). The discussion is balanced and acknowledges uncertainties.
